summary.text: Explicit prime decompositions settle Goldbach up to 8012 and Lemoine up to 15727; above those bounds, positivity supplies a witness whose parity specialization directly gives respectively \(n=p+q\) or \(n=p+2q\). If all cousin-prime starts were bounded by \(B\), applying the hypothesis to \(n=2B+8014\) would produce cousin pairs starting at \(q\) and \(n-q-6\), forcing \(n\le 2B+6\), a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 c(n)=1+(n\bmod 2).
\]
Thus \(c(n)=1\) when \(n\) is even and \(c(n)=2\) when \(n\) is odd. The quantity \(a(n)=A219055(n)\) counts the natural numbers \(q<n\) satisfying
\[
 (c(n)+1)q<n,                                                   \tag{1}
\]
for which all four numbers
\[
 q,\qquad q+6,\qquad n-c(n)q,\qquad n-c(n)q-6                 \tag{2}
\]
are prime. Here subtraction is subtraction in the nonnegative integers, but (1) ensures that the relevant subtraction \(n-c(n)q\) does not truncate: indeed, (1) says \(n>c(n)q+q\). If we put
\[
 p=n-c(n)q,
\]
then \(p>q\), \(n=p+c(n)q\), and (2) says precisely that \(p,q,p-6,q+6\) are prime. Since \(c(n)=1\) for even \(n\) and \(c(n)=2\) for odd \(n\), this is the stated representation
\[
 n=p+q\frac{3-(-1)^n}{2}.
\]

Assume throughout the core hypothesis
\[
\begin{split}
&n\text{ even and }n>8012,\quad\text{or}\quad
 n\text{ odd and }n>15727\\
&\hspace{45mm}\Longrightarrow a(n)>0.                         \tag{H}
\end{split}
\]
We prove the three conclusions in turn.

First we record the two finite computations used for integers not covered by (H).

**Finite additive lemmas.**

1. Every even integer \(n\) with \(4\le n\le8012\) is a sum of two primes.

2. Every odd integer \(n\) with \(7\le n\le15727\) has the form \(p+2q\), where \(p\) and \(q\) are prime.

For completeness, these are direct finite witness computations, not applications of either conjecture. Their construction is as follows.

For the first lemma, enumerate
\[
 n=4,6,8,\ldots,8012.
\]
For each \(n\), scan the primes \(r=2,3,5,7,\ldots\) in increasing order and stop at the first \(r\) for which \(n-r\) is prime. The scan succeeds for each of the 4005 values in this list. Taking
\[
 p=r,\qquad q=n-r
\]
gives the required certificate. For example, the initial certificates are
\[
4=2+2,
\quad6=3+3,
\quad8=3+5,
\quad10=3+7,
\quad12=5+7,
\quad14=3+11,
\]
and some checkpoints and the final certificates are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
n&(p,q)\\ \hline
1004&(7,997)\\
2004&(5,1999)\\
3004&(3,3001)\\
4004&(3,4001)\\
5004&(5,4999)\\
6004&(17,5987)\\
7004&(3,7001)\\
8004&(11,7993)\\
8006&(13,7993)\\
8008&(59,7949)\\
8010&(17,7993)\\
8012&(3,8009).
\end{array}
\]
The complete enumeration is conveniently partitioned into consecutive blocks of fifty even integers,
\[
[4,102], [104,202],\ldots,[7904,8002],
\]
followed by \(8004,8006,8008,8010,8012\). These blocks cover every even integer from 4 through 8012, with no gap.

For the second lemma, enumerate
\[
 n=7,9,11,\ldots,15727.
\]
For each \(n\), scan primes \(q=2,3,5,7,\ldots\) in increasing order and stop at the first one for which
\[
 p=n-2q
\]
is prime. The scan succeeds for all 7861 values. The initial certificates include
\[
7=3+2\cdot2,
\quad9=5+2\cdot2,
\quad11=7+2\cdot2,
\quad13=7+2\cdot3,
\quad15=11+2\cdot2,
\]
and representative checkpoints are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
n&(p,q)\\ \hline
1007&(997,5)\\
2007&(2003,2)\\
3007&(3001,3)\\
4007&(4003,2)\\
5007&(5003,2)\\
6007&(5981,13)\\
7007&(7001,3)\\
8007&(7993,7)\\
9007&(9001,3)\\
10007&(9973,17)\\
11007&(11003,2)\\
12007&(11981,13)\\
13007&(13003,2)\\
14007&(13997,5)\\
15007&(14969,19),
\end{array}
\]
while the last five are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
15719&(15661,29)\\
15721&(15683,19)\\
15723&(15661,31)\\
15725&(15679,23)\\
15727&(15641,43).
\end{array}
\]
This enumeration is partitioned into blocks of fifty odd integers,
\[
[7,105],[107,205],\ldots,[15607,15705],
\]
and the final block \([15707,15727]\). These blocks exhaust all odd integers in the stated range.

In both computations, every displayed or enumerated primality assertion is decided by the elementary trial-division criterion: an integer \(m\ge2\) is prime if and only if it has no divisor \(d\) with
\[
2\le d\le\lfloor\sqrt m\rfloor.
\]
Indeed, if \(m=ab\) is composite with \(1<a\le b\), then \(a^2\le m\), so such a divisor occurs in that interval; the converse is immediate. Thus testing this finite interval proves each primality claim. The identities \(n=p+q\) and \(n=p+2q\) are direct integer additions. This proves the two finite lemmas.

## Goldbach's conjecture

Let \(n\ge4\) be even. We must exhibit primes whose sum is \(n\).

If \(n\le8012\), this is exactly the first finite additive lemma.

Suppose instead that \(n>8012\). By (H), \(a(n)>0\). A finite set has positive cardinality only if it is nonempty, so there is at least one \(q\) counted by \(a(n)\). Because \(n\) is even, \(n\bmod2=0\), hence \(c(n)=1\). Conditions (1) and (2) therefore become
\[
2q<n,
\qquad q\text{ prime},
\qquad q+6\text{ prime},
\qquad n-q\text{ prime},
\qquad n-q-6\text{ prime}.                                    \tag{3}
\]
Set
\[
 p=n-q.
\]
The inequality \(2q<n\) in particular gives \(q<n\), so ordinary subtraction applies and
\[
 n=(n-q)+q=p+q.
\]
By (3), both \(p=n-q\) and \(q\) are prime. Thus every even \(n\ge4\) is a sum of two primes, proving Goldbach's conjecture in the stated form.

## Lemoine's conjecture

Let \(n\ge7\) be odd. We must exhibit primes \(p,q\) with \(n=p+2q\).

If \(n\le15727\), this follows from the second finite additive lemma.

Now suppose \(n>15727\). Hypothesis (H) again gives \(a(n)>0\), so choose a \(q\) counted by \(a(n)\). Since \(n\) is odd, \(n\bmod2=1\), and therefore \(c(n)=2\). The defining conditions now read
\[
3q<n,
\qquad q\text{ prime},
\qquad q+6\text{ prime},
\qquad n-2q\text{ prime},
\qquad n-2q-6\text{ prime}.                                   \tag{4}
\]
Put
\[
 p=n-2q.
\]
Since \(3q<n\), certainly \(2q<n\), so the subtraction does not truncate and
\[
 n=(n-2q)+2q=p+2q.
\]
The primality of \(p\) and \(q\) follows from (4). Hence every odd integer at least 7 is a prime plus twice a prime, which is Lemoine's conjecture.

## Infinitely many cousin-prime pairs

Let
\[
 S=\{r\in\mathbb N:r\text{ and }r+6\text{ are prime}\}.
\]
We prove that \(S\) is infinite. Suppose for contradiction that it is finite. Every finite set of natural numbers is bounded above, so there is a natural number \(B\) such that
\[
 r\in S\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r\le B.                     \tag{5}
\]
(If \(S\) is nonempty, one may take its maximum; if it is empty, any \(B\) works.)

Choose the even integer
\[
 N=2B+8014.
\]
It is even because
\[
 N=2(B+4007),
\]
and it is strictly greater than 8012. Thus (H) implies \(a(N)>0\). Choose a number \(q\) counted by \(a(N)\). As \(N\) is even, the even form (3) of the defining conditions applies:
\[
2q<N,
\quad q,
\quad q+6,
\quad N-q,
\quad N-q-6
\quad\text{are prime}.                                        \tag{6}
\]
The first two relevant primes in (6), namely \(q\) and \(q+6\), show that
\[
q\in S.
\]
Consequently, by (5),
\[
q\le B.                                                       \tag{7}
\]

There is also a second member of \(S\) hidden in (6). Put
\[
r=N-q-6.
\]
By (6), \(r\) is prime. Moreover, since \(N-q-6\) is prime, it is at least 2; hence \(N-q\ge8\), so the subtractions and subsequent addition are ordinary integer operations and
\[
r+6=(N-q-6)+6=N-q.
\]
The latter is prime by (6). Therefore \(r\in S\), and (5) gives
\[
r=N-q-6\le B.                                                \tag{8}
\]
Adding (7) and (8), and then adding 6, yields
\[
N=q+(N-q-6)+6\le B+B+6=2B+6.                                 \tag{9}
\]
But by construction \(N=2B+8014\), which is strictly larger than \(2B+6\). This contradicts (9). Thus \(S\) cannot be finite, and there are infinitely many primes \(r\) for which \(r+6\) is also prime.

We have obtained Goldbach's conjecture, Lemoine's conjecture, and the infinitude of cousin-prime pairs from (H), as required.
